rationale: A wins because it finds the cleanest business story and keeps the proof holes visible instead of decorating them. Its strongest headline, "The poster child of online-only retail now runs more than 300 stores," is a real contrarian retail angle with a defined beat, clock, and evidence test. B has useful material, but "LensCrafters, EssilorLuxottica, Pearle Vision" and "direct shot at the incumbents' moat" import an optical-industry fight the supplied update does not prove. That is how a decent angle gets turned into homework for the reporter.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker was the canonical example of that thesis" is plausible industry context, but it is not in the supplied update; this needs either sourcing or softer framing.
"Warby Parker's founding pitch was eliminating the middleman" is outside the provided facts, even if likely true. Do not make the angle depend on unsupplied brand history without proof.
"pharmacy chains' fight to reinvent the front of store" adds a broader news frame not supplied in the update; it may be right, but it needs evidence before pitching.
gaps_in_B: "LensCrafters, EssilorLuxottica, Pearle Vision" are named external competitors not supplied in the update; that specificity looks smart until a reporter asks where it came from.
"the historically defensible, insurance-tied part of the optical business the incumbents have owned" is an asserted industry thesis, not a fact from the update.

"a direct shot at the incumbents' moat" overstates the evidence. Forty stores with mostly optometrist-staffed exams does not prove a competitive attack without market, pricing, insurance, or incumbent-response data.
The first and third angles both revolve around in-store eye exams; the competitive lens and retail-health lens are different, but the set is still leaning on the same fact twice.
